Drager on the return

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
The Drager alcohol testing machine was perfect for law enforcement officers trying to get quick, easy convictions in court for drunken driving. The machine measured alcohol content and blood did not have to be taken. But 5 years ago in a huge High Court case in Cape Town, Drager was outlawed as it was shown there were some issues with it and its accuracy could not be determined as 100 per cent accurate.

This was a huge set back with massive knock-on effects. Blood would have to be sent to national laboratories and would take ages to get back. Cases would fall by the way side.

But it is on its way back now and about to be re-launched. We find out what they have done to make this more accurate. And what it means for law enforcement.

Press Release:


Dräger Breathalysers
When the innovative Dräger breathalyser was introduced across the Western Cape, it was seen as the perfect tool to swiftly convict drunk drivers. But the accuracy of the device was successfully challenged in the Cape High Court. This resulted in a ban on the apparatus, severe backlogs in blood tests and delayed court cases. But it’s making a comeback and very soon drunk drivers could face conviction based solely on the strength of a breathalyser result. Carte Blanche asks: could it be an effective deterrent against drunk driving?


Script:


DRAGER RETURNS SCRIPT

Another regular road block in Cape Town this last week where traffic officers were on the alert to nab drivers over the Alcohol Limit or drunk. According to the world health organization South Africa tops the list of drunken driving related deaths in the world. Official statistics last year show that roughly 14000 motorists and pedestrians died on South African Roads. The Medical Research Council believes that figure that figure could be as high as 18 000.

John: How significant a problem is drunken driving?
Donald Grant: We know it has, we think, more than 60% effect.

60% then of all our road deaths are as a result of drunken driving. Besides the human cost, the cost to our economy is staggering.

Donald Grant: We talking here about, I know for the Western Cape, it is about 21 Billion a year and the country estimated 306 Billion.

Presently like at this roadblock last week in Cape Town, motorists are screened in their vehicles for being over the limit. If the first reading shows positive, another test is performed. If the reading is then over the prescribed limit of 34mg per thousand milliliters the driver is arrested and taken away for blood testing.

Inspector Maxine Jordaan who has been part of many roadblocks is frustrated because the wheels of justice then turn so slowly.

Maxine Jordaan: It would take up to 3 -18 months for an officer to be subpoenaed to court. In most instances the cases get struck off the court roll because the blood takes so long to come back from the laboratory.

Caro Smit knows all about the effects of lengthy court processes. She lost her son Chas in 2005 when he was run over by a woman she alleges was drunk. She started an NGO called South Africans Against Drunk Driving.

Caro Smit: It can take 3-5 Years and the trauma is there all the time. They having to go to court if they, so it’s tremendously hard for the families to have the cases last so long.

LINK: But all that is about to change with the imminent reappearance of the device called the Drager Alcotest. It was introduces in the Western Cape back in 2010 and was seen as the provincial government then as a major weapon in the fight against drunk driving.

The Drager Alcotest Breathalyzer fist made its appearance as long ago as 1953 when a German company developed a device that measured the levels of Alcohol in the breath. It has since been used by law enforcement agencies around the world. It was first introduced in South Africa in 1996 and used in Gauteng and Natal. A Pietermaritzburg judge in 2010 ruled that the results were admissible in court, which reaffirmed that there was no need for conventional blood testing and its inherent delays.

The National Forensic Laboratories are testing up to 120 000 samples of blood per year from drivers suspected of being over the limit. MEC Donald Grant says that the Drager became a deterrent for motorists considering driving under the influence.

Donald Grant: We saw the levels of fatalities drop from about 1744 in 2010 down to under 1200 so there was a rapid decline.

Cape Town drivers knew how rapid justice had become. This was a typical Friday night at the Shadow Centre where drivers who were found to be over the limit were taken to be tested by the Drager Alcotest Breathalyzer. Realizing they were over the limit, some refused to blow into the machine and then had to be held down forcibly for their blood to be drawn.

LINK: But in 2011 the provincial government and the drager were dealt a significant blow. Things came to a head in the western cape high court in case known as the state vs. Clifford Hendricks.

In 2010 Capetonian Clifford Hendricks was arrested for driving over the legal limit. He challenged the validity of the Drager alcotest Breathalyzer in the high court. Forensic Analyst David Klatzow assisted with the defense.

David Klatzow: Remember you are dealing with peoples lives here, you are dealing with people who could be found guilty of a criminal offence and it can have long term, huge implications for the rest of their lives.

This test case saw top legal minds pitted against each other.

John: Why do you think it was that such heavy weights were called into the case?
David Klatzow: Because what they wanted to do and it was quite clear from the word go is they wanted this to be a one horse race and they wanted to get a judgment in the high court which would be binding on the lower courts. So it was a stitch up.

MEC Donald Grant saw the case differently.

Donald Grant: It was actually at the instance of the provincial government that we looked for a test case, because many of the minor courts were actually throwing a lot of these cases out. So we wanted, because courts are there to interpret the law.

In September 2011 Judge Nathan Erasmus found that the state had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the results produced by the Drager Alcotest Breathalyzer were conclusive proof that Hendricks was over the limit. He was acquitted.

The defense had proved that the reliability of the apparatus was in question as was the training of those who operated it. However the judge did not rule out the future use of the Drager Alcotest Breathalyzer in the fight against drunken driving. He said, "There appears no reason in principle why an evidential breath test, properly applied, could not be such a tool."

After that judgment it was back to conventional blood testing and the delays as experienced by Capetonian Gavin Bell who in 2012 was pulled over in the early hours of the morning after running a red robot. He was arrested and his blood was drawn and sent for testing.

Gavin Bell: IT took a full three years to actually get all of my case over and done with and getting my blood results.

His case came to a conclusion only in November last year.

LINK: They say that justice delayed is justice denied and very often the focus is on the perpetrator but of course the delay in getting the results of blood tests has a major impact on the families of the victims too.

John: As somebody who has lost a son and who also hears stories from other victims, you must be incredibly frustrated how the lab system has appeared to deteriorate and the length of time it takes to get blood results back?
Caro Smit: I am you know, basically every time somebody is killed and it is in the paper, it like hits me personally and if you even look at the western cape the deaths had gone down by 30% when the evidential breathalyzer was used. Once it stopped, the deaths have gone up by 10%


This week we approached the national forensic laboratories for information about the backlog. They claim that currently the average turn around time for new incoming samples is only six to eight weeks. And good news for Caro, but bad news for drivers who insist on driving over the limit is that since the judgment in 2011 the Western Cape government has been closely working behind the scenes. On Wednesday MEC Donald Grant proudly showed us the latest model of the alcotest Breathalyzer, which he is confident, will stand up in court.

Donald Grant: We are very grateful to judge Erasmus. Its a very technical judgment and it is one of the reasons why it has taken us so long with the all the agencies in play with the all the agencies in play and there are 9 of them that we have had to consult over this time together with the manufacturers of the equipment as well as actually educating and retraining our officers in terms of the use of the equipment.

Graeme Matthews: We did work with government and with all the authorities involved to obviously get a device that is for local standards as well.

Graeme Matthew’s teams have been hard at work training officers around the country.

Graeme Matthews: We will supply the instructor's training from the various traffic colleges. It has been looked at, it has been approved and this is for the use and the functionality of the machine. From then those officials will get trained at the traffic colleges as an operator and that will be part of their competency test as well.

D. Klatzow remains a little bit skeptical and believes that blood testing remains the most accurate measurement.

John: So what is the solution do you think?
David Klatzow: Sort the labs out. The labs were perfectly able to function and you can use Breathalyzer to weed out those who need blood testing from those who don’t and it is very simple. Make certain the labs work correctly

John: How are you feeling now that it appears we are going to push ahead with the drager?
Caro Smit: Absolutely thrilled because one of the big deterrents of drink drivers is if they get swift sentencing so we will have the swift sentencing.

Gavin Bell: Going through to court and hearing the clanging of the keys and the jail cells behind you and the screaming. It was extremely traumatic.

For Bell justice was far from swift and it still haunts him. He was not convicted but ordered to undergo community service. He wrote an article about his experience.

Gavin Bell: If I can get somebody to understand that the process that they are going to take, that if they drink and drive, there is a possibility that they could kill somebody, there is a possibility that they going to get a criminal record.

Donald Grant: My biggest wish to the driving public out there is to just understand we are not out to get you.

Rather than creating more criminals, MEC Grant hope the drager will be a powerful deterrent.

Donald Grant: What we want to do is reduce the carnage on our roads and we believe that this took could change behavior where people are saying hang on, there is a chance that if I drink over the weekend, A I am going to spend the weekend in jail and B I may in court within 3 days with the consequences.
